metadata.title: EAU Guidelines on Sexual and Reproductive Health
metadata.summary: This section addresses the classification, assessment and management of male ejaculatory disorders. It covers premature ejaculation, delayed ejaculation, anejaculation, painful ejaculation, retrograde ejaculation, anorgasmia and haemospermia. Management topics include psychosexual and pharmacological treatment, procedures, fertility-related interventions and risk-based investigation.

target_population: Men who have sex with men (MSM)

toxicities.incidence: Treatment-emergent adverse events led to discontinuation in 4% of subjects receiving 30 mg and 10% receiving 60 mg.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Adverse effects were dose-dependent; dose titration must be considered.

toxicities.incidence: Phase 3 studies reported vasovagal syncope at a rate of 0.1%. A post-marketing observational study reported no syncope cases.
prevention: Measure orthostatic blood pressure and heart rate before starting dapoxetine.
Use medical history and orthostatic testing to identify patients at risk of an orthostatic reaction.

toxicities.incidence: With on-demand clomipramine 15 mg, nausea was reported in 15.7% of men and dizziness in 4.9% of men.

toxicities.dose_modifications: The adverse effects are usually mild and tend to improve after two to three weeks of treatment.

prevention: Prescribing SSRIs warrants caution in adolescents aged ≤ 18 years with PE and in men with PE and a coexisting depressive disorder, particularly when suicidal ideation is present.
Advise patients not to stop daily SSRIs abruptly or reduce their dose rapidly.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Avoid abrupt cessation or rapid dose reduction of daily SSRIs.

prevention: Men with PE who are trying to conceive should avoid SSRIs.
Couples seeking parenthood should not use topical lidocaine/prilocaine-containing substances because these chemicals may harm fresh human sperm cells.

toxicities.event: Partner vaginal numbness and allergy to topical anaesthetic ingredients
recognition: Vaginal numbness after transfer of the cream or gel to the partner
Allergy to a product ingredient in the patient or partner
prevention: Use a condom after applying the cream, or wash the penis to remove residual product before intercourse.
Do not use topical anaesthetics when the patient or partner is allergic to any ingredient.

toxicities.incidence: Genital hypoaesthesia occurred in 4.5% of men and 1.0% of female partners; ED occurred in 4.4% of men; vulvovaginal burning sensation occurred in 3.9% of female partners.

toxicities.event: Adverse effects and potential for addiction or breathing difficulty
prevention: Use tramadol cautiously for PE because long-term safety data in this setting are lacking, including data on addiction potential.
toxicities.dose_modifications: Constipation, sedation and dry mouth were reported at doses used for analgesia (≤ 400 mg daily); no toxicity-based dose adjustment is specified.

toxicities.incidence: Randomised controlled studies reported no serious treatment-emergent adverse events related to hyaluronic acid glans injections.
prevention: Use hyaluronic acid injection cautiously relative to more established PE treatments; further safety studies are needed before recommending it to patients with PE.
Do not perform dorsal neurectomy because additional safety data are needed.

toxicities.dose_modifications: The reported treatment-emergent effects were minimal and did not result in discontinuation.

toxicities.event: Dryness of mucous membranes and hypertension
Significant adverse effects reported with pharmacotherapy for anorgasmia
prevention: The evidence is not strong enough to recommend these drugs for anorgasmia; reported efficacy is limited and adverse-effect profiles are significant.

prophylaxis.recommendation: Check orthostatic blood pressure and heart rate before dapoxetine treatment, and consider dose titration to minimise syncope risk.
After applying lidocaine/prilocaine cream, use a condom or wash residual product from the penis before intercourse to avoid transfer to the partner.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients using lidocaine/prilocaine cream and their partners

prophylaxis.recommendation: Avoid SSRIs because of their detrimental effects on sperm cells.
prophylaxis.target_population: Men with PE who are trying to conceive

prophylaxis.recommendation: Do not use topical lidocaine/prilocaine-containing substances because they may have cytotoxic effects on fresh human sperm cells.
Avoid abruptly stopping daily SSRIs or rapidly reducing their dose because withdrawal syndrome may occur.

infection_management.management: When PE coexists with a genitourinary infection, treat the infection first. If infection is identified as a cause of painful ejaculation, appropriate antibiotic treatment may improve the pain.

infection_management.pathogen_or_syndrome: Urogenital infections or STIs associated with haemospermia
infection_management.management: Give appropriate antibiotic therapy when a urogenital infection or STI is present.

conditions.name: Premature ejaculation
conditions.description: Early ejaculation involves ejaculation before or shortly after vaginal penetration or another relevant sexual stimulus, with little perceived control. The pattern occurs episodically or persistently for at least several months and causes clinically significant distress. Diagnosis also considers ejaculation latency, perceived control and interpersonal consequences.
conditions.epidemiology: Estimates of prevalence have been limited by differing definitions. The National Health and Social Life Survey reported that prevalence did not vary with age or marital or income status. PE was more common in Black men, Hispanic men and men from regions where an Islamic background is common; prevalence may also be higher with lower educational attainment. Few affected men seek treatment.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Patients may report reduced satisfaction with intercourse and their sexual relationship, difficulty relaxing during intercourse, less frequent intercourse, diminished self-confidence, relationship strain, distress, anxiety, embarrassment or depression. A partner’s sexual functioning and relationship satisfaction may also be affected. ED can coexist with PE or contribute to secondary PE.

subtypes.name: lifelong PE
subtypes.distinguishing_features: PE present from the outset of sexual experience; the document proposes a possible interaction of central and peripheral serotonergic, dopaminergic, oxytocinergic, endocrinological, genetic and epigenetic factors.

subtypes.name: acquired PE
subtypes.distinguishing_features: PE arising after a period without the problem; possible contributors include performance anxiety, relationship or other psychological difficulties, ED, prostatitis, hyperthyroidism and poor sleep quality.

subtypes.name: Variable PE
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Irregular, inconsistent episodes of early ejaculation that represent normal variation in sexual performance.

subtypes.name: Subjective PE
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A perception of rapid ejaculation despite latency within, or longer than, the normal range; it should not be treated as evidence of a medical disorder.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish onset, duration, consistency, situational circumstances, sexual stimulation, effects on sexual activity and QoL, medication or substance use, perceived ejaculatory control, distress and interpersonal difficulty.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Distinguish lifelong from acquired PE, situational from consistent PE, and PE from ED or PE secondary to ED.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise ejaculation latency during vaginal intercourse.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Routine clinical assessment when IELT is applicable.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Self-estimation is sufficient in everyday practice, but IELT alone cannot define PE and is unsuitable for some non-coital sexual activities. Self-estimated and stopwatch-measured IELT assigned PE status with 80% sensitivity and 80% specificity.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Measure ejaculation latency as an outcome in clinical trials.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: For drug studies, a cited proposal favours geometric rather than arithmetic mean IELT because the distribution is skewed.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess control, frequency, response to minimal stimulation, distress and interpersonal difficulty.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When a patient-reported diagnostic measure is used.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A total score > 11 suggests PE; 9 or 10 suggests probable PE; < 8 indicates a low likelihood.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess desire, erection sufficient for intercourse, ejaculation timing and control, patient and partner satisfaction, and anxiety or depression.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When a patient-reported diagnostic and severity measure is used.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A cut-off score of 30 (range 7-35) best discriminates PE. Severity categories are severe (score: 7-13), moderate (score: 14-19), mild-tomoderate (score: 20-25) and mild (score: 26-30).

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise PE and assess treatment outcomes.
Characterise PE and assess treatment effects.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise PE and assess treatment effects.
Assess PE in the context of masturbation.
Identify anatomical abnormalities or urological, endocrine or neurological conditions associated with PE or other sexual dysfunctions, particularly ED.
Investigate a specific suspected underlying condition.

conditions.name: lifelong PE
conditions.description: A form of PE distinguished by its presence throughout sexual life; it may be generalised or situational.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Early ejaculation with limited perceived control and associated distress, beginning from the outset of sexual experience.

subtypes.name: lifelong generalised
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A lifelong category of early ejaculation designated as generalised.

subtypes.name: lifelong situational
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A lifelong category associated with particular circumstances or a particular partner.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether PE has been lifelong and whether it is generalised or situational; assess latency, control, distress and interpersonal effects.
Assess latency when applicable.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: IELT alone is insufficient to establish PE.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify associated anatomical abnormalities or other sexual dysfunctions.

conditions.name: acquired PE
conditions.description: A form of PE developing after a preceding period without early ejaculation; it may be generalised or situational.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Early ejaculation may occur alongside performance anxiety, other psychological or relationship difficulties, ED, prostatitis, hyperthyroidism or poor sleep quality.

subtypes.name: acquired generalised
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An acquired category of early ejaculation designated as generalised.

subtypes.name: acquired situational
subtypes.distinguishing_features: An acquired category occurring under particular circumstances or with a particular partner.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify when PE began, its situational pattern, possible triggers, underlying conditions and effects on the patient and partner.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Assess whether difficulty obtaining or maintaining an erection underlies the complaint.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Explore anxiety, guilt, fear of being caught, rapid masturbation, psychosexual development, attention and control issues, interpersonal anxiety and effects on the partner.
Identify abnormalities or conditions associated with PE and other sexual dysfunctions.
Investigate a suspected underlying condition.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Only if specific history or examination findings direct testing.

conditions.name: Variable PE
conditions.description: A proposed PE syndrome consisting of intermittent, irregular early ejaculation that is considered normal variation in sexual functioning.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Episodes of rapid ejaculation occur inconsistently rather than forming a stable pattern.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish that episodes are variable and distinguish this pattern from other PE subtypes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An inconsistent pattern may represent normal sexual variation.

conditions.name: Subjective PE
conditions.description: A proposed PE syndrome in which ejaculation is perceived as too rapid despite latency being within the normal range or longer; it is not considered a manifestation of a medical pathology.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The perceived rapid ejaculation may be consistent or inconsistent. Cultural or psychological constructs may contribute.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Compare perceived ejaculation speed with the reported pattern and latency.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The subjective complaint can coexist with normal or longer ejaculation latency.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterise latency when applicable.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: IELT must be considered alongside perceived control and distress rather than used alone.

conditions.name: Delayed Ejaculation (DE)
conditions.description: The cited American Psychiatric Association definition requires marked delay, infrequency or absence of ejaculation on 75-100% of occasions for at least 6 months, with personal distress. A cited study found that latency and control, but not bother or distress, significantly differentiated affected men from those without ejaculatory disorders.
conditions.epidemiology: On limited evidence, estimated prevalence is around 1% for lifelong DE and 4% for acquired DE.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Ejaculation may be substantially delayed or infrequent. Possible contributing factors include psychological difficulties, neurological or anatomical injury, medications, altered tactile sensitivity, tissue atrophy, idiosyncratic masturbation and lack of desire for available stimuli. More recent studies did not confirm an association between ejaculation time and serum testosterone levels.

subtypes.name: lifelong DE
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Present throughout sexual life. In a cited study, affected men were younger, reported more DE symptoms, were less likely to have a causative medical condition or medication, and were more likely to masturbate to reduce anxiety or distress rather than for pleasure than men with acquired delayed ejaculation.

subtypes.name: acquired DE
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Develops after a preceding period without DE.

subtypes.name: situational DE
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A recognised pattern whose occurrence depends on the situation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the ejaculatory response, sensation, frequency, sexual activities and techniques, cultural context, onset, desire, arousal, ejaculation, orgasm, refractory period, partner’s perspective and sexual functioning, and relationship satisfaction.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Identify potentially contributing medical, medication-related and psychological factors.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate possible medical or anatomical contributors.

diagnostic_workup.test: Assessment of hormonal milieu, anatomy and overall medical condition
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify medical pathologies that cause or contribute to DE.

conditions.name: Anejaculation
conditions.description: Complete absence of both antegrade and retrograde ejaculation due to failure of semen emission into the urethra from the seminal vesicles, prostate and ejaculatory ducts.
conditions.clinical_presentation: True anejaculation usually occurs with preserved orgasmic sensation and is associated with central or peripheral nervous system dysfunction or medication use. Its potential causes overlap with those of DE and retrograde ejaculation.

conditions.name: Painful Ejaculation
conditions.description: Discomfort or pain of varying intensity occurring during or after ejaculation.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Pain can affect the penis, scrotum or perineum. Reported possible contributors include genitourinary conditions, procedures, pelvic radiation, drugs, toxins and psychological difficulties; some cases have no identified cause. A psychological cause may be relevant when pain does not occur during masturbation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a condition or exposure to which treatment can be directed.

conditions.name: Retrograde ejaculation
conditions.description: Complete or partial loss of antegrade ejaculation when semen instead passes through the bladder neck into the bladder.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Orgasmic sensation may be normal or reduced. Infertility is a major concern. The document groups potential causes as neurogenic, urethral, pharmacological, endocrine and related to bladder neck incompetence.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Recover sperm from urine for assisted reproduction.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Infertility management when this sperm-acquisition method is selected.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The collected specimen is centrifuged and the recovered material resuspended for possible use in assisted reproductive techniques.

conditions.name: Anorgasmia
conditions.description: A perceived absence of orgasm, whether or not ejaculation occurs; it can lead to anejaculation.
conditions.epidemiology: The document attributes 90% of anorgasmia problems to psychological factors.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Possible factors include substance abuse, obesity, anxiety and fear. The condition is often discussed alongside ejaculatory disorders, particularly DE.

subtypes.name: Primary anorgasmia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Begins with a man’s first sexual intercourse and continues throughout life.

subtypes.name: secondary anorgasmia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Begins after a period of normal orgasmic function.

diagnostic_workup.test: Detailed physical and psychosexual assessment of the patient and partner
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Establish onset, disease and medication history, penile sensitivity and psychological issues.
Help exclude an organic cause.
Help exclude an organic cause.
Help exclude an organic cause.

diagnostic_workup.test: Further investigation of penile sensitivity loss
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate reduced penile sensation.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When the patient has loss of penile sensitivity.

conditions.name: Haemospermia
conditions.description: Blood appearing in the ejaculate. Although often associated with a minor cause, it may indicate underlying disease and can cause considerable anxiety.
conditions.epidemiology: The reported risk of any malignancy among patients presenting with haemospermia is approximately 3.5% (0-13.1%). In a study of 342 patients, inflammation or infection accounted for 49.4% of cases, whereas genitourinary cancers accounted for 3.2%. The document notes that most cases arise from infection or another inflammatory process.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Blood in the ejaculate may be isolated, recurrent or persistent, and may occur with other symptoms or haematuria. Apparent haemospermia can instead reflect haematuria or a partner’s blood entering the urethra during intercourse.

subtypes.name: idiopathic
subtypes.distinguishing_features: No cause is identified.

subtypes.name: congenital malformations
subtypes.distinguishing_features: The document includes SV or ejaculatory duct cysts among possible causes.

subtypes.name: inflammatory conditions
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Possible causes include genitourinary inflammation and infection.

subtypes.name: obstruction
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Possible causes include calculi, cysts, stricture and BPH.

subtypes.name: malignancies
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Possible tumours involve the prostate or other genitourinary sites.

subtypes.name: vascular abnormalities
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Possible causes include varices, telangiectasia, haemangioma and posterior urethral veins.

subtypes.name: iatrogenic/trauma
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May follow injury or a procedure, including prostate biopsy.

subtypes.name: systemic causes
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Possible contributors include hypertension, bleeding disorders and other systemic disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm that blood originates in the ejaculate; assess duration, recurrence, STI exposure, travel to areas affected by schistosomiasis or tuberculosis, systemic illness and possible malignancy symptoms.
Identify signs of an underlying condition.
Assess for hypertension as a possible associated condition.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate urinary findings and possible infection.
Investigate suspected tuberculosis or schistosomiasis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Test for Chlamydia, Ureaplasma and Herpes Simplex virus.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Investigation of a possible sexually transmitted cause.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An infectious cause may be identified in a case that otherwise might have been classified as idiopathic.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In appropriately counselled men aged > 40 years; the management algorithm specifies prostate cancer screening in men ≥ 40 years old.

Contribute to the initial assessment.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Clinical assessment; also included with PSA in prostate cancer screening for men ≥ 40 years old in the management algorithm.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An association between haemospermia and PCa has been proposed but is not fully established.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: In a prospective study of 106 patients with prolonged haemospermia, the diagnostic yield for TRUS was 45.3%; combining transrectal US with seminal vesiculoscopy established a diagnosis in 87.7%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate structural changes and help locate the origin of midline or paramedian prostatic cysts and plan surgery.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Included in the higher-risk pathway of the management algorithm.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An endorectal coil can improve accuracy in locating a haemorrhage and its possible cause.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Suggested for high-risk features, including persistent haemospermia refractory to conservative treatment; the algorithm places cystourethroscopy ± biopsy after recurrence.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Considered as an investigative technique in a cited prospective study.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: In men < 40 years old on the higher-risk pathway of the management algorithm.

diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When distinguishing melanospermia is clinically necessary.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Melanospermia has been reported in association with malignant melanoma involving the genitourinary tract.

prognostic_tools.name: risk-stratification system
components: Isolated versus recurrent or persistent haemospermia
Associated symptoms or signs of disease
Actual risk for PCa, including positive family history

risk_groups.criteria: Men < 40 years old with an isolated episode and no other symptoms or signs of disease.
Men ≥ 40 years old, or a man of any age with persistent haemospermia or associated symptoms or signs of disease.

prognostic_tools.interpretation: The proposed management algorithm uses risk grouping to guide the extent of investigation and management.

recommended_tests: Cystourethroscopy ± biopsy after recurrence in the management algorithm

decision_rules: Establish the PE subtype and discuss treatment expectations before starting therapy.
If ED, another sexual dysfunction, or a genitourinary infection is present, treat that condition first; PE secondary to ED may be treated after or alongside ED.

recommended_regimens.name: Dapoxetine
recommended_regimens.summary: Approved on-demand oral first-line treatment in many countries, but not in the USA. The studied doses were 30 mg or 60 mg taken 1-2 hours before intercourse.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Across patients, 30 mg and 60 mg increased IELT 2.5- and 3.0-fold, respectively; among patients whose baseline average IELT was < 30 seconds, the corresponding increases were 3.4- and 4.3-fold. RCTs also found better ejaculatory control and satisfaction and less distress.

recommended_regimens.name: Lidocaine/prilocaine spray
recommended_regimens.summary: Approved topical first-line option for lifelong PE; studies administered three sprays 5 min before intercourse.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Published studies reported an increase in IELT of up to 6.3-fold over 3 months, with improvement in patient-reported outcomes.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: On demand, 5 min before sexual intercourse

response_assessment.method: Self-estimated IELT, perceived ejaculatory control, distress and interpersonal difficulty
response_assessment.interpretation: IELT alone does not adequately characterise PE.

supportive_care: Provide patient counselling and education and discuss treatment choices.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Long-term outcomes of pharmacological treatment are unknown. Before starting dapoxetine, measure orthostatic blood pressure and heart rate and consider dose titration because of syncope risk.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with PE for whom an alternative to approved first-line treatment is appropriate
decision_rules: Daily SSRIs or daily or on-demand clomipramine are viable off-label second-line alternatives.

recommended_regimens.name: SSRIs
recommended_regimens.summary: Use off-label daily oral treatment. Continuous regimens described include citalopram, fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, paroxetine and sertraline; the guide also describes daily or on-demand SSRI use as effective.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Meta-analyses suggest an increase in geometric mean IELT of 2.6-13.2-fold. Paroxetine produced greater ejaculation delay than fluoxetine, clomipramine and sertraline; sertraline was superior to fluoxetine.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Daily treatment; delay may begin after a few days and becomes more apparent after one to two weeks

recommended_regimens.name: clomipramine
recommended_regimens.summary: Use off-label daily or on demand. An RCT studied 15 mg taken 2-6 hours before sexual intercourse.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In the cited RCT, the treatment group had a greater IELT fold change and better patient-reported measures than placebo (4.66 ± 5.64 vs. 2.80 ± 2.19, P < 0.05). Comparative analyses found no significant efficacy difference between clomipramine and fluoxetine or sertraline.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Daily or on demand; the cited on-demand RCT administered treatment 2-6 hours before sexual intercourse

alternative_regimens.name: Lidocaine/prilocaine cream
alternative_regimens.summary: Topical anaesthetic treatment can delay ejaculation; transfer to the partner can cause vaginal numbness.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: When considering an off-label topical option; avoid if the patient or partner is allergic to a product ingredient or if the couple is seeking parenthood.

response_assessment.method: Assess ejaculation delay and tolerability during antidepressant treatment.
response_assessment.interpretation: The delay may become more evident over this period; tachyphylaxis may occur after six to twelve months.

supportive_care: Advise patients taking daily SSRIs against abrupt cessation or rapid dose reduction.
For topical cream, use a condom after application or wash residual compound off the penis before intercourse to reduce partner exposure.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Use caution with SSRIs in adolescents aged ≤ 18 years and in men with comorbid depression, particularly with suicidal ideation. Patients trying to conceive should avoid these antidepressants because of reported detrimental effects on sperm cells; couples seeking parenthood should not use topical lidocaine/prilocaine-containing substances.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with PE considering an alternative to on-demand or daily antidepressants
decision_rules: Consider off-label on-demand tramadol cautiously as a viable third-line alternative.

recommended_regimens.name: Tramadol
recommended_regimens.summary: Use cautiously on demand as an off-label third-line option rather than an established first-line treatment. Trials assessed tramadol ODT (62 and 89 mg) and tramadol HCI.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Studies of on-demand treatment reported increases of up to 2.5-fold in median IELT.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence for long-term safety in PE is inadequate, including the potential for addiction. The document also notes a warning about breathing difficulty.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with acquired PE, particularly when ED, prostatitis, LUTS, anxiety, hyperthyroidism, another sexual dysfunction or genitourinary infection contributes to symptoms
decision_rules: Identify the underlying cause and make its treatment the initial goal.
Treat ED, other sexual dysfunction or genitourinary infection first; if PE is secondary to ED, ED treatment may also proceed concurrently with PE treatment.

recommended_regimens.name: Treatment of the underlying cause
recommended_regimens.summary: Address the identified condition contributing to acquired PE before prioritising PE-specific treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: Psychological/behavioural therapies combined with pharmacological treatment
alternative_regimens.summary: Use combined treatment in acquired PE; psychosexual approaches may address ejaculatory control, anxiety and difficulties within the couple.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: When treating acquired PE with pharmacotherapy; the recommendation for combined psychological or behavioural treatment is graded Weak.

response_assessment.method: Assess ejaculatory symptoms, perceived control, distress and the effect on the relationship.

supportive_care: Discuss expectations, provide sexual education and include the partner when available.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence for psychosexual interventions alone is weak and inconsistent, and their long-term outcomes are unknown.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with variable or subjective PE, or men who are uncomfortable with pharmacological therapy
decision_rules: Consider behavioural techniques for variable or subjective PE.
Psychotherapy may be considered instead of pharmacotherapy when the patient is uncomfortable with medication, or alongside medication.

alternative_regimens.name: Psychosexual interventions
alternative_regimens.summary: Behavioural, cognitive, couple-based or psycho-educational approaches may address ejaculation control, sexual confidence, anxiety and communication. Discuss mindfulness exercises; evidence suggests that start-stop exercises combined with psycho-education and mindfulness improve symptoms and associated distress, anxiety and depression.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Variable or subjective PE, reluctance to use medication, or use alongside pharmacotherapy; evidence for psychosexual treatment alone remains weak and inconsistent.

response_assessment.method: Assess PE symptoms and associated distress, anxiety and depression.

supportive_care: Consider the partner's experience and participation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Variable PE is described as a normal variation of sexual function; subjective PE should not be treated as evidence of a true medical pathology. Long-term outcomes of psychosexual interventions are unknown.

decision_rules: PDE5Is may be used alone or with other treatments in patients who have PE without ED.

recommended_regimens.name: PDE5Is
recommended_regimens.summary: Use alone or in combination with other PE treatment. The document reports that sildenafil improved confidence, perceived control and sexual satisfaction and reduced anxiety, although IELT did not improve significantly in the studies discussed.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: IELT was not significantly improved with sildenafil in the cited studies.

alternative_regimens.name: PDE5Is and SSRIs
alternative_regimens.summary: Open-label studies and a Bayesian network meta-analysis found the combination more effective than SSRI monotherapy.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Combination treatment for PE.

alternative_regimens.name: dapoxetine with sildenafil
alternative_regimens.summary: An RCT in men with PE without ED reported significantly better IELT and patient-reported outcomes with the combination than with either drug alone, with tolerable adverse events.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Men with PE without ED considering combination pharmacotherapy.

response_assessment.method: Assess IELT, perceived ejaculatory control, satisfaction and anxiety.
response_assessment.interpretation: Improvement in patient experience need not coincide with a significant increase in IELT.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men considering a procedural option for PE
decision_rules: Use hyaluronic acid injection cautiously relative to more established treatments.
Do not perform dorsal neurectomy because further safety data are needed.

alternative_regimens.name: hyaluronic acid injection
alternative_regimens.summary: Glans injections reduced penile sensitivity; randomised controlled studies reported a modest but significant IELT increase and improved patient-reported measures. Serious complications remain possible.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: A cautiously considered option compared with more established modalities; the recommendation is graded Weak, and further safety studies are needed.

not_recommended.name: dorsal neurectomy
not_recommended.reason: The guide recommends against performing this irreversible procedure because additional safety data are required; recommendation grade: Weak.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Other proposed modalities, including penis-root masturbation, vibrator-assisted start-stop exercises, transcutaneous functional electric stimulation, transcutaneous posterior tibial nerve stimulation, acupuncture and yoga, need more evidence before clinical use can be considered.

decision_rules: Investigate potential psychological, organic and medication-related contributors before selecting treatment.
No definitive treatment is supported by sufficient evidence.

alternative_regimens.name: Psychological treatment
alternative_regimens.summary: Possible approaches include genital-specific stimulation, sexual education, changes to masturbation practices, anxiety reduction and addressing a mismatch between fantasy and partnered arousal. Referral to a sexual therapist, psychologist or psychiatrist is appropriate and often warranted.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: When psychological or psychosexual contributors are identified; empirical evidence of treatment efficacy is scarce.

alternative_regimens.name: penile vibratory stimulation (PVS)
alternative_regimens.summary: Used as an adjunct for DE. A study combining midodrine with PVS in 158 men with spinal cord injury produced ejaculation in almost 65% of patients.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Adjunctive treatment, including in men with spinal cord injury.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Agents used with varied success include cabergoline, bupropion, pseudoephedrine, midodrine, imipramine, ephedrine, buspirone, oxytocin, testosterone, bethanechol, yohimbine, amantadine, cyproheptadine and apomorphine. None has proven efficacy or superiority because adequate comparative trials are lacking; no medication is approved for DE by the FDA or EMA.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with anejaculation after lymphadenectomy or neuropathy, men with spinal cord injury, and the cases of anorgasmia discussed in this treatment pathway
decision_rules: Use PVS first; eliciting the ejaculation reflex requires an intact lumbosacral spinal cord segment.
If PVS fails, electro-ejaculation may be selected. If electro-ejaculation fails or is not feasible, consider other sperm-retrieval techniques.

recommended_regimens.name: PVS
recommended_regimens.summary: First-line application of a vibrator to the penis to evoke ejaculation.

alternative_regimens.name: electro-ejaculation
alternative_regimens.summary: May be the treatment of choice after unsuccessful PVS.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: PVS failure.

alternative_regimens.name: Other sperm-retrieval techniques
alternative_regimens.summary: Options for obtaining sperm when electro-ejaculation cannot be performed or does not succeed.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Electro-ejaculation failure or infeasibility.

alternative_regimens.name: in vitro fertilisation
alternative_regimens.summary: The couple may enter a programme when fatherhood is desired and semen quality is poor or ejaculation is retrograde.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Desire for fatherhood with poor-quality semen or retrograde ejaculation.

not_recommended.name: Drug treatment for anejaculation caused by lymphadenectomy and neuropathy, or psychosexual therapy for anorgasmia
not_recommended.reason: The guide states that these treatments are not effective in the cases described.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Anejaculation after retroperitoneal surgery for testicular cancer or total mesorectal excision may be prevented with unilateral lymphadenectomy or autonomic nerve preservation, respectively.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with painful ejaculation and an identifiable underlying cause
decision_rules: Tailor treatment to the cause that is found.

recommended_regimens.name: Treatment of the underlying cause
recommended_regimens.summary: Depending on the cause, psychotherapy or relationship counselling, withdrawal of a suspected drug or other agent, or suitable antibiotics, α-blockers or anti-inflammatory agents may relieve symptoms.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with painful ejaculation for whom no underlying cause is identified
decision_rules: Consider symptom-directed measures when evaluation does not identify a cause.

alternative_regimens.name: Behavioural therapy, muscle relaxants, antidepressant treatment, anticonvulsant drugs and/or opioids, and pelvic floor exercises
alternative_regimens.summary: These are possible approaches for painful ejaculation without an identified cause.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: No underlying cause identified.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with painful ejaculation after unsuccessful medical treatment
decision_rules: Surgical procedures have been suggested after medical treatment fails, but should be used cautiously.

alternative_regimens.name: TURP, transurethral resection of the ejaculatory duct (TURED) or neurolysis of the pudendal nerve
alternative_regimens.summary: Surgical options suggested for persistent symptoms; strong evidence that surgery improves painful ejaculation is lacking.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Medical treatment failure; use with caution.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men seeking restoration of antegrade ejaculation, including those with ejaculatory failure after retroperitoneal lymphadenectomy
decision_rules: Sympathomimetics are pharmacological options for restoring antegrade ejaculation.
Antimuscarinics have also been used alone or with sympathomimetics, but studies are too small for statistical comparison of combination treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: synephrine, pseudoephedrine hydrochloride, ephedrine, phenylpropanolamine and midodrine
alternative_regimens.summary: Common sympathomimetics described for retrograde ejaculation. A systematic review found efficacy of 28% for this medication group; their effect diminishes over time.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Pharmacological attempt to restore antegrade ejaculation.

alternative_regimens.name: brompheniramine maleate and imipramine
alternative_regimens.summary: Antimuscarinics used alone or together with sympathomimetics; calculated efficacy was 22% for antimuscarinics alone and 39% for combination treatment.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Considered as pharmacological treatment, with or without sympathomimetics.

response_assessment.timepoint: After four days of treatment prior to ejaculation
response_assessment.interpretation: In the cited RCT after retroperitoneal lymphadenectomy, this pretreatment duration was most effective among those studied.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Evidence includes small studies and case reports. Sympathomimetics can cause dry mucous membranes and hypertension.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with retrograde ejaculation seeking fertility treatment
decision_rules: Consider sperm acquisition from post-ejaculatory urine, the Hotchkiss technique or ejaculation with a full bladder; standard testicular sperm aspiration/extraction (TESA/TESE) techniques are also described.

alternative_regimens.name: Centrifugation and resuspension
alternative_regimens.summary: Dilute or alkalise urine through increased fluid intake or sodium bicarbonate, obtain post-orgasmic urine, then centrifuge and resuspend the specimen for assisted reproduction. A systematic review reported a pregnancy rate per cycle of 15% (0-100%).
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Sperm acquisition for assisted reproduction.

alternative_regimens.name: Hotchkiss method
alternative_regimens.summary: Empty and wash the bladder before ejaculation, instil Lactated Ringers, then retrieve semen after ejaculation; modified techniques vary the instillation medium. Reported pregnancy rates were 24% per cycle (0-100%).
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Sperm acquisition for fertility treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: Ejaculation on a full bladder
alternative_regimens.summary: Ejaculate with a full bladder and suspend the recovered semen in Baker’s Buffer. The guide cites two studies including only five patients without stating a pregnancy-rate value.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Sperm acquisition for fertility treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: TESA/TESE
alternative_regimens.summary: Standard sperm-retrieval techniques mentioned as additional options.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Fertility management.

decision_rules: Assess the patient and partner physically and psychosexually, including onset, medications, disease history, penile sensitivity and psychological concerns.
Psychological and behavioural approaches resemble those used for DE.

alternative_regimens.name: Lifestyle changes and psychotherapy
alternative_regimens.summary: Possible measures include altering masturbation style, improving intimacy, reducing alcohol consumption, changing arousal methods, addressing sexual anxiety, role-playing an exaggerated orgasm and increasing genital stimulation. Success rates are difficult to establish.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Psychological or behavioural management of anorgasmia.

not_recommended.name: Drugs to treat anorgasmia
not_recommended.reason: Current evidence is not strong enough to recommend pharmacotherapy; reports involving cyproheptadine, yohimbine, buspirone, amantadine and oxytocin generally come from case-cohort studies and describe limited efficacy and significant adverse effects.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Adjunctive tests may help exclude organic causes; patients with reduced penile sensitivity require further investigation.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men with anorgasmia seeking sperm retrieval after the described treatments fail
decision_rules: If prior treatment is unsuccessful, consider methods of obtaining sperm.

alternative_regimens.name: penile vibratory stimulation
alternative_regimens.summary: Option for sperm retrieval after treatment failure.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Unsuccessful preceding treatment.

alternative_regimens.name: electro-ejaculation
alternative_regimens.summary: Option for sperm retrieval after treatment failure.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Unsuccessful preceding treatment.

alternative_regimens.summary: Option for sperm retrieval after treatment failure.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Unsuccessful preceding treatment.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men aged < 40 years with a single episode of haemospermia and no other symptoms or signs of disease
decision_rules: Confirm true haemospermia, assess for an underlying cause and exclude serious disease.
Use conservative management and watchful waiting in the low-risk group; reassure the patient if evaluation finds no pathology.

recommended_regimens.name: Conservative treatment and watchful waiting
recommended_regimens.summary: Primary management for a low-risk isolated episode after appropriate evaluation, with reassurance if no pathology is identified.

response_assessment.method: Reassess risk and the need for further investigation.
response_assessment.interpretation: Recurrent or persistent haemospermia is a higher-risk feature.

supportive_care: Address the patient's anxiety while avoiding unnecessary investigation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The main treatment objective is to exclude malignancy and address any cause found.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Men aged ≥ 40 years, or men of any age with persistent haemospermia or accompanying symptoms or signs of disease; recurrent haemospermia, concurrent haematuria and PCa risk are additional higher-risk features
decision_rules: Investigate higher-risk presentations more thoroughly and treat an identified cause.
If symptoms recur or persist despite conservative management, consider further evaluation, including cystourethroscopy ± biopsy as shown in the management algorithm.

recommended_regimens.name: Cause-directed treatment
recommended_regimens.summary: Give appropriate antibiotics for urogenital infection or STI; treat systemic disease appropriately. Urethral or prostate varices or angiodysplastic vessels may be fulgurated, seminal-vesicle or prostatic-urethral cysts may be aspirated transrectally, and ejaculatory duct obstruction may be treated by transurethral incision at the duct opening.

response_assessment.method: Re-evaluate for an underlying cause and consider cystourethroscopy ± biopsy.
response_assessment.interpretation: Persistent or recurrent symptoms warrant consideration of further investigation.

supportive_care: Explain the risk assessment and address anxiety while avoiding unnecessary investigation.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: In middle-aged patients with recurrent haemospermia, the guide calls for more aggressive intervention. Evaluation aims to exclude serious causes, particularly malignancy, while treating any condition identified.

therapies_index.name: dapoxetine
therapies_index.mechanism: Short-acting SSRI that delays ejaculation.
approved_indications: On-demand treatment of lifelong and acquired PE in many countries, but not in the USA.
therapies_index.administration: 30 mg or 60 mg orally, 1-2 hours before intercourse.
key_toxicities: Dose-dependent nausea, diarrhoea, thirst, headache and dizziness.
Vasovagal syncope was reported at a rate of 0.1% in phase 3 studies.
ED is described as a possible treatment-related concern.
monitoring: Measure orthostatic blood pressure and heart rate before treatment.

therapies_index.name: lidocaine/prilocaine spray
therapies_index.mechanism: Delivers a concentrated film to the glans penis to reduce neural sensitivity while limiting numbness.
approved_indications: EMA-approved on-demand treatment of lifelong PE.
therapies_index.administration: Metered-dose aerosol containing lidocaine (150 mg/mL) and prilocaine (50 mg/mL); three sprays 5 min before sexual intercourse.
key_toxicities: Genital hypoaesthesia was reported in 4.5% of men and 1.0% of female partners.
ED was reported in 4.4%.
Vulvovaginal burning sensation was reported in 3.9%.

therapies_index.name: lidocaine/prilocaine cream
therapies_index.mechanism: Topical anaesthesia reduces glans sensitivity and delays ejaculation.
therapies_index.administration: Apply topically to the penis; use a condom afterward or wash off residual product before intercourse.
key_toxicities: Transfer to a partner may cause vaginal numbness.
Lidocaine/prilocaine-containing substances may harm fresh human sperm cells.

therapies_index.name: lidocaine
therapies_index.mechanism: Topical anaesthesia reduces glans sensitivity.
therapies_index.administration: The document describes topical use in combination with prilocaine and as a lidocaine-only spray.

therapies_index.name: prilocaine
therapies_index.mechanism: Topical anaesthesia reduces glans sensitivity.
therapies_index.administration: Used topically in combination with lidocaine.

therapies_index.name: Lidocaine-only sprays
therapies_index.mechanism: Topical anaesthesia reduces glans sensitivity.
therapies_index.administration: Topical spray for PE; no dose or timing is specified.

therapies_index.name: SSRIs

therapies_index.administration: Daily or on-demand use for PE is described as off-label. Avoid abrupt cessation or rapid dose reduction when taken daily.
key_toxicities: Fatigue, drowsiness, yawning, nausea, vomiting, dry mouth, diarrhoea and perspiration.
Decreased libido, anorgasmia, anejaculation and ED.
Potential withdrawal syndrome after abrupt cessation or rapid dose reduction.
Potential suicidal ideation or suicide attempts in the populations for which prescribing caution is advised.
Detrimental effects on sperm cells.

therapies_index.name: tramadol

document_sections.heading: 6. DISORDERS OF EJACULATION
document_sections.content: The chapter covers premature, delayed, absent, painful and retrograde ejaculation, as well as anorgasmia and haemospermia.

document_sections.heading: 6.1 Introduction
document_sections.content: Ejaculation involves emission and expulsion, coordinated through neurological and hormonal pathways. Disruption of these pathways can produce premature ejaculation (PE), retarded or delayed ejaculation, anejaculation, painful ejaculation, retrograde ejaculation, anorgasmia or haemospermia.

document_sections.heading: 6.2 Premature ejaculation
document_sections.content: This section addresses the frequency, possible causes, effects, classification, assessment and management of PE.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.1 Epidemiology
document_sections.content: Historical prevalence estimates are difficult to compare because surveys lacked a universally accepted definition of PE. Section 4.2 discusses its epidemiology in greater detail.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.2 Pathophysiology and risk factors
document_sections.content: The cause of PE remains relatively uncertain. Evidence for proposed biological and psychological explanations, including anxiety, penile hypersensitivity and 5-hydroxytryptamine (HT) receptor dysfunction, is limited. Classifying PE into lifelong, acquired, variable and subjective subtypes has helped distinguish these presentations. A proposed explanation for lifelong PE involves interacting central and peripheral serotonergic, dopaminergic, oxytocinergic, endocrine, genetic and epigenetic influences. Acquired PE may arise with performance anxiety, other psychological or relationship difficulties, ED, prostatitis, hyperthyroidism or poor sleep quality. Variable PE is regarded as normal variation in sexual function; subjective PE may reflect cultural or atypical psychological constructs. A significant proportion of men with ED also have PE. Anxiety about ED may aggravate PE and lead clinicians to miss the underlying ED. In the National Health and Social Life Survey (NHSLS), PE prevalence did not vary with age, unlike ED, which became more frequent with age. Marital and income status did not affect PE prevalence. PE was more common in Black men, Hispanic men and men from regions where an Islamic background is common; prevalence may also be greater with lower educational attainment. Other reported risk factors are genetic predisposition, poor general health, obesity, prostate inflammation, hyperthyroidism, low prolactin, high testosterone, vitamin D and B12 deficiency, diabetes, MetS, physical inactivity, emotional difficulties, stress, depressive symptoms and traumatic sexual experiences.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.3 Impact of PE on quality of life
document_sections.content: Men with PE more often report dissatisfaction with their sexual relationship and intercourse, difficulty relaxing during intercourse and less frequent intercourse. PE may harm confidence and the partner relationship and can cause distress, anxiety, embarrassment or depression. A partner's sexual functioning may also be affected, while their relationship satisfaction declines as the patient's PE becomes more severe. Despite potentially serious psychological and quality-of-life effects, few affected men seek care.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.4 Classification
document_sections.content: Definitions and classification of PE still lack substantial consensus, although PE is broadly understood to encompass several related concepts. International Classification of Diseases 11th Revision uses the term Early Ejaculation for ejaculation before, or very shortly after, vaginal penetration or other relevant sexual stimulation, with little or no perceived control. Its definition also requires an episodic or persistent pattern lasting at least several months and clinically significant distress. Its categories are male early ejaculation, lifelong generalised and situational, acquired generalised and situational, and unspecified. Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders V (DSM-V) and International Society for Sexual Medicine (ISSM) definitions of lifelong and acquired PE overlap in 3 diagnostic dimensions: latency assessed by IELT, perceived control, and distress or related frustration and interpersonal difficulty. Two further proposed syndromes are variable PE, involving irregular episodes of early ejaculation within normal sexual variation, and subjective PE, involving a perception of rapid ejaculation despite normal or even longer latency. Subjective PE should not be treated as evidence of a genuine medical pathology.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.5 Diagnostic evaluation
document_sections.content: Diagnosis rests on medical and sexual history. History should distinguish lifelong from acquired PE and situational from consistent PE, and address ejaculation time, stimulation, effects on sexual activity and quality of life, and drug use or misuse. Clinicians should differentiate PE from ED: erection-related anxiety can produce secondary PE, while some patients mistake the normal loss of erection after ejaculation for ED when PE is their actual concern.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.5.1 Intravaginal ejaculatory latency time (IELT)
document_sections.content: IELT has been proposed as an objective diagnostic and outcome measure, but cannot establish PE on its own because values overlap considerably between men with and without PE. It is unsuitable for assessing PE during masturbation, oral sex or anal intercourse. PE appears less prevalent and less troublesome among men who have sex with men (MSM), but MSM can experience it and IELT cannot be applied to them. Studies disagree on whether MSM have longer ejaculation latency than straight men. Self-estimated IELT is adequate in routine practice. Self-estimation and stopwatch measurement identify PE status interchangeably, with 80% sensitivity and 80% specificity. Calibrated-stopwatch measurement is required in clinical trials. For PE drug studies, Waldinger et al. proposed geometric rather than arithmetic mean IELT because its distribution is skewed; using the arithmetic mean could overstate treatment-related delay.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.5.2 Premature ejaculation assessment questionnaires
document_sections.content: Several PROMs-based questionnaires assess PE, but only Premature Ejaculation Diagnostic Tool (PEDT) and Arabic Index of Premature Ejaculation (AIPE) distinguish men with PE from those without it. PEDT has five items addressing control, frequency, minimal stimulation, distress and interpersonal difficulty. A total > 11 suggests PE, 9 or 10 suggests probable PE, and < 8 indicates low likelihood. AIPE has seven items covering desire, erections sufficient for intercourse, latency, control, patient and partner satisfaction, and anxiety or depression. Its best diagnostic cut-off is 30 (range 7-35); severity categories are severe (score: 7-13), moderate (score: 14-19), mild-tomoderate (score: 20-25) and mild (score: 26-30). Premature Ejaculation Profile (PEP), Index of Premature Ejaculation (IPE) and Male Sexual Health Questionnaire Ejaculatory Dysfunction (MSHQ-EjD) can characterise PE or assess treatment effects, but are optional in daily practice. Masturbatory Premature Ejaculation Diagnostic Tool (MPEDT) has been proposed because affected men report longer IELTs and less distress during masturbation than partnered sex; further validation is needed before routine use in this population.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.5.3 Physical examination and investigations
document_sections.content: Initial assessment may include a focused urological, endocrine and neurological examination to identify conditions associated with PE or other sexual dysfunction, including endocrinopathy, Peyronie’s disease, urethritis and prostatitis. Laboratory and physiological investigations should follow specific historical or examination findings rather than be ordered routinely.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.5.4 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the diagnostic evaluation of PE
document_sections.content: Evidence at LE 3 indicates that comprehensive history and examination can help identify medical contributors to PE; LE 2a indicates possible harm to confidence, relationships and mental health; LE 2b supports PEDT and AIPE for diagnosis and PEP for treatment assessment; and LE 3 supports self-reported IELT in routine care while finding IELT alone insufficient for characterisation. The recommendations are to diagnose and classify PE using medical and sexual history, including self-estimated IELT, perceived control, distress and interpersonal difficulties (Strong); use patient-reported outcomes in routine practice (Weak); include examination at initial assessment to detect anatomical abnormalities associated with PE or other sexual dysfunction, particularly ED (Strong); and avoid routine laboratory or physiological investigations, reserving them for specific historical or examination findings (Strong).

document_sections.heading: 6.2.6 Disease management
document_sections.content: Before treatment, clinicians should establish the PE subtype and discuss the patient's expectations thoroughly. Pharmacotherapy must be considered first-line for lifelong PE; for acquired PE, initial management must address causes such as ED, prostatitis, LUTS, anxiety or hyperthyroidism. Behavioural techniques may help variable and subjective PE. Psychotherapy can be considered when a patient is uncomfortable with medication or alongside medication, although evidence for psychosexual interventions is weak and inconsistent and their long-term outcomes are unknown. Dapoxetine (30 and 60 mg) is the first approved on-demand oral agent for lifelong and acquired PE in many countries, but not the USA. An on-demand metered-dose aerosol combining lidocaine (150 mg/mL) and prilocaine (50 mg/mL) is the first topical product approved by the EMA in the European Union for lifelong PE. Other medicines used for PE are off-label. Daily or on-demand selective serotonin re-uptake inhibitors (SSRIs) and clomipramine, and on-demand topical anaesthetics, have consistently shown efficacy. Long-term pharmacological outcomes remain unknown. The chapter presents an evidence-based analysis, evidence levels, recommendation grades and a management algorithm.

document_sections.heading: Figure 6.1: Management of premature ejaculation
document_sections.content: The algorithm begins with a clinical diagnosis informed by patient history and, where available, partner history. It considers IELT, perceived ejaculatory control, bother or stress, onset and duration, psychosocial and relationship concerns, medical history and examination. Management includes counselling, education and discussion of options. When PE is secondary to ED, ED is treated first or at the same time. Pharmacotherapy is the recommended first-line option for lifelong PE: approved on-demand choices are dapoxetine and lidocaine/prilocaine spray; listed off-label choices are chronic daily antidepressants (SSRIs or clomipramine) and on-demand tramadol. Combining medication with behavioural therapy is another pathway.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.6.1 Psychological aspects and intervention
document_sections.content: Behavioural, cognitive and couple-focused psychosexual approaches aim to develop ejaculatory control, strengthen sexual confidence, reduce anxiety and improve communication and problem-solving between partners. Sexual education or acceptance-focused work may help. Psychosexual treatment alone lacks empirical support. Recent evidence suggests start-stop exercises combined with psycho-education and mindfulness improve PE symptoms and related distress, anxiety and depression; potential mindfulness benefits have also been reported. Behavioural work may contribute most when added to medical treatment. A smartphone-delivered intervention targeting delay skills and sexual confidence produced positive effects, supporting E-health approaches for PE.

document_sections.heading: Figure 6.2: Key aspects for psychosexual evaluation
document_sections.content: The assessment considers specific triggers in acquired PE, including anxiety, guilt, fear of discovery and rapid masturbation. It reviews psychosexual history and development, involves the partner where possible and examines effects on that partner. It also evaluates dysfunctional thinking and attention, control concerns and interpersonal anxiety, then considers referral for sexual psychotherapy with active partner involvement.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.6.1.1 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the assessment and treatment (psychosexual approach) of PE
document_sections.content: Evidence at LE 2b associates psychosexual approaches combined with psycho-education and mindfulness with improvement in PE symptoms, distress, anxiety and depression. LE 3 indicates better outcomes when psychosexual and pharmacological approaches are combined than with medication alone. Recommendations are to assess sexual history and psychosexual development (Strong), evaluate anxiety and interpersonal anxiety while focusing on control issues (Strong), and involve an available partner and assess the effect of PE on them (Strong). For treatment, behavioural, cognitive and/or couple therapy should be combined with pharmacotherapy, with mindfulness exercises discussed (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.2.6.2 Pharmacotherapy
document_sections.content: The following subsections review approved and off-label medicines, combinations, emerging interventions, comparative results, adverse effects and limitations of the evidence for PE.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.6.2.1 Dapoxetine
document_sections.content: Dapoxetine hydrochloride is a short-acting SSRI suitable for on-demand PE treatment, with Tmax of 1.3 hours and a 95% clearance rate after 24 hours. It is approved in European countries and elsewhere, but not the USA. Doses of 30 mg and 60 mg produced overall IELT increases of 2.5- and 3.0-fold, respectively; in patients whose baseline average IELT was < 30 seconds, increases were 3.4- and 4.3-fold, respectively. RCTs using 30 mg or 60 mg 1-2 hours before intercourse found longer IELT, better perceived control and satisfaction, and less distress. Efficacy was similar for lifelong and acquired PE. Dose-dependent adverse effects included nausea, diarrhoea, thirst, headache and dizziness. Treatment-emergent adverse events led to discontinuation in 4% of participants receiving 30 mg and 10% receiving 60 mg. Studies showed no indication of increased suicidal thoughts or attempts and little indication of withdrawal after abrupt cessation. The guide describes dapoxetine as safer than formal antidepressant compounds used for PE. Phase 3 studies reported vasovagal syncope at 0.1%. Product information requires orthostatic blood pressure and heart-rate measurement before treatment and consideration of dose titration. The EMA concluded that adequate risk minimisation made the potentially increased syncope risk manageable. A post-marketing observational study using history and orthostatic testing to identify at-risk patients observed no syncope. Some patients and physicians may prefer combining dapoxetine with a PDE5I to prolong latency and reduce the risk of treatment-related ED. Phase 1 studies found no pharmacokinetic interaction with tadalafil 20 mg or sildenafil 100 mg. Coadministration with PDE5Is was well tolerated, with a safety profile consistent with earlier phase 3 dapoxetine-only studies. An RCT in PE without ED found that dapoxetine plus sildenafil significantly improved IELT and PROs relative to either drug alone, with tolerable adverse events. Efficacy and safety have also been reported for dapoxetine/sildenafil combination tablets. Discontinuation appears moderate to high, with cumulative discontinuation reaching 90% at 2 years. Reported reasons were cost (29.9%), disappointment that PE was not curable and with on-demand dosing (25%), adverse effects (11.6%), perceived poor efficacy (9.8%), seeking other options (5.5%) and unknown reasons (18.3%). Another report described spontaneous discontinuation among dapoxetine users, compared with rates of 50% for other SSRIs and 28.8% for paroxetine. In a Chinese cohort, 13.6% stopped dapoxetine; among those stopping, reasons were lack of efficacy (62%), adverse effects (24%) and infrequent intercourse (14%).

document_sections.heading: 6.2.6.2.2 Off-label use of antidepressants
document_sections.content: SSRIs, originally used for mood disorders, have been used off-label for PE since the 1990s because they can delay ejaculation. Continuously administered citalopram, fluoxetine, fluvoxamine, paroxetine and sertraline have similar efficacy, although paroxetine produces the greatest delay. GSK958108, a 5-HT1A receptor antagonist, significantly delayed ejaculation in a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial. Clomipramine, described as the most serotoninergic tricyclic antidepressant, was first reported effective for PE in 1977. In a recent RCT, clomipramine 15 mg taken on demand 2-6 hours before intercourse was associated with IELT fold change and significantly improved PRO measures versus placebo (4.66 ± 5.64 vs. 2.80 ± 2.19, P < 0.05). Nausea in 15.7% and dizziness in 4.9% were its most commonly reported treatment-emergent adverse events. Meta-analyses suggest SSRIs may raise geometric mean IELT by 2.6-13.2-fold. Paroxetine outperformed fluoxetine, clomipramine and sertraline; sertraline outperformed fluoxetine; and clomipramine did not differ significantly from fluoxetine or sertraline. Evaluated doses were paroxetine 20-40 mg, sertraline 25-200 mg, fluoxetine 10-60 mg and clomipramine 25-50 mg. Delay can begin a few days after treatment starts and becomes more evident after one to two weeks, as receptor desensitisation takes time. Efficacy may persist for several years, but tachyphylaxis may arise after six to twelve months. Common SSRI adverse events include fatigue, drowsiness, yawning, nausea, vomiting, dry mouth, diarrhoea and perspiration; these are usually mild and gradually improve after two to three weeks. Reduced libido, anorgasmia, anejaculation and ED have also been reported. Because of suicidal thoughts or attempts, caution is suggested when prescribing SSRIs for adolescents aged ≤ 18 years with PE or for men with PE and comorbid depression, particularly with suicidal ideation. Patients should be advised against abruptly stopping or rapidly reducing daily SSRIs because withdrawal syndrome may occur. Patients attempting conception should avoid these medicines because of adverse effects on sperm cells.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.6.2.3 Topical anaesthetic agents
document_sections.content: Local anaesthesia is the oldest pharmacological approach to delaying ejaculation. Trials support the hypothesis that topical desensitisation reduces glans sensitivity and increases latency without impairing the sensation of ejaculation. Meta-analyses confirm efficacy and safety. For treatment lasting < 8 weeks, one meta-analysis ranked local anaesthetics highest in efficacy among the assessed options, which included SSRIs, dapoxetine 30 and 60 mg, PDE5Is and tramadol.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.6.2.3.1 Lidocaine/prilocaine cream
document_sections.content: Lidocaine/prilocaine cream can significantly increase stopwatch-measured IELT from 1-2 minutes to 6-9 minutes. No significant treatment-emergent adverse events have been reported, but allergy to any product ingredient in the patient or partner is a contraindication. Cream or gel can transfer to a partner and cause vaginal numbness; patients are therefore advised to use a condom after application or wash residual product from the penis before intercourse. Couples seeking parenthood should avoid topical lidocaine/prilocaine-containing products because these chemicals may be cytotoxic to fresh human sperm.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.6.2.3.2 Lidocaine/prilocaine spray
document_sections.content: The EMA-approved eutectic metered-dose spray for lifelong PE contains lidocaine (150 mg/mL) and prilocaine (50 mg/mL) in base forms. Compared with cream, its controlled delivery creates a concentrated film over the glans, maximising neural blockade while minimising onset of numbness and avoiding absorption through penile-shaft skin. Studies found improved IELT and PROs with three sprays administered 5 min before intercourse. Published long-term data reported IELT increases up to 6.3-fold over 3 months, improving month by month. Reported local adverse events included genital hypoaesthesia in 4.5% of men and 1.0% of female partners, ED in 4.4%, and vulvovaginal burning in 3.9%; systemic adverse events were considered unlikely. Lidocaine-only sprays are also available and have shown efficacy for PE.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.6.2.4 Tramadol
document_sections.content: Tramadol is a centrally acting analgesic with opioid-receptor activation and inhibition of serotonin and noradrenaline re-uptake. It is a mild opioid-receptor agonist with antagonistic activity at noradrenaline and 5-HT transporters, distinguishing it from other opioids, including morphine. Oral absorption is ready and elimination half-life is 5-7 hours. Trials assessed tramadol ODT (62 and 89 mg) and tramadol HCI for PE. On-demand treatment produced reported median IELT increases of up to 2.5-fold. Adverse effects at analgesic doses (≤ 400 mg daily) included constipation, sedation and dry mouth. In May 2009, the US FDA warned of addiction and breathing difficulty. Tolerability during a twelve-week PE study was acceptable, while other studies found significant dose-related efficacy alongside potential adverse effects. The Guidelines Panel considers tramadol a possible alternative to established first-line options, but says it must be used cautiously because long-term safety data in PE are lacking.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.6.2.5 Phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitors
document_sections.content: Sildenafil did not significantly increase IELT, but increased confidence, perceived ejaculatory control and overall sexual satisfaction while reducing anxiety and the time needed to obtain a second erection after ejaculation. Open-label studies, subsequently supported by a Bayesian network meta-analysis, found PDE5Is combined with SSRIs more effective than SSRI monotherapy.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.6.2.6 Other drugs
document_sections.content: Research continues into additional PE treatments. Selective α-blockers have been studied because of α1a-adrenergic receptors in the seminal vesicles and prostate and the sympathetic system's role in ejaculation. One study suggested modafinil may delay ejaculation and improve PROMs. Hyaluronic acid glans augmentation was proposed to reduce penile sensitivity in 2004 and has become popular mainly in Asian countries. Randomised controlled studies reported safe injections, a modest but significant IELT increase and improved PRO measures, without serious injection-related treatment-emergent adverse events. Nevertheless, serious complications may occur, and further safety studies are needed before recommending the procedure. Selective dorsal neurectomy has also been proposed, primarily by Asian investigators; its irreversible nature warrants more safety data. Studies of oxytocin receptor antagonists were prompted by the importance of central oxytocin receptors to the ejaculation reflex. Epelsiban and cligosiban appeared safe and mildly effective, but require further controlled trials. Delayed ejaculation was observed as a side-effect of pregabalin. On-demand oral pregabalin 150 mg increased patient IELTs 2.45 ± 1.43-fold; blurred vision, dizziness and vomiting were minimal and caused no discontinuations. Penis-root masturbation, vibrator-assisted start-stop exercises, transcutaneous functional electric stimulation, transcutaneous posterior tibial nerve stimulation, acupuncture and yoga require more evidence before clinical adoption for PE.

document_sections.heading: 6.2.7 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the treatment of PE
document_sections.content: At LE 1a, the evidence summary identifies on-demand dapoxetine and eutectic lidocaine/prilocaine spray as the only approved PE medications, alongside off-label daily or on-demand SSRIs and clomipramine; finds significant IELT improvement and generally tolerable adverse effects with on-demand dapoxetine or daily SSRIs; finds significant IELT improvement and generally tolerable adverse effects with daily or on-demand clomipramine; considers tramadol effective but its long-term safety evidence, including addiction risk, insufficient; and finds PDE5Is plus SSRIs more effective than SSRIs alone. At LE 1b, lidocaine/prilocaine creams and sprays significantly improve IELT and have a safe profile. At LE 2b, hyaluronic acid injections reduce penile sensitivity. Recommendations are to treat ED, other sexual dysfunction or genitourinary infection such as prostatitis first (Strong); use dapoxetine or lidocaine/prilocaine spray first-line for lifelong PE (Strong); consider off-label daily oral SSRIs or daily/on-demand clomipramine viable second-line alternatives (Strong); use off-label on-demand tramadol cautiously as a viable third-line alternative to on-demand or daily antidepressants (Strong); use PDE5Is alone or with other therapies in PE without ED (Strong); combine psychological or behavioural therapy with medication for acquired PE (Weak); use hyaluronic acid injections cautiously relative to better-established PE treatments (Weak); and avoid dorsal neurectomy because more safety information is needed (Weak).

document_sections.heading: 6.3 Delayed Ejaculation (DE)
document_sections.content: This section addresses DE definition, possible causes, assessment and treatment.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.1 Definition and classification
document_sections.content: The American Psychiatric Association definition requires marked delay, infrequency or absence of ejaculation on 75-100% of occasions for at least 6 months, with personal distress. A recent study found latency and control useful for distinguishing DE from no ejaculatory disorder, but did not find bother or distress significant. DE may be lifelong, acquired or situational. A recent study found that, compared with acquired DE, lifelong DE involved younger age, greater symptoms, lower likelihood of a causative medical condition or medication, and greater likelihood of masturbating to reduce anxiety or distress rather than for pleasure. Evidence is limited, but estimated prevalence is around 1% for lifelong DE and 4% for acquired DE.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.2 Pathophysiology and risk factors
document_sections.content: Possible causes of DE include psychological factors, organic conditions such as incomplete spinal cord lesions or iatrogenic penile nerve injury, and medicines including SSRIs, antihypertensives and antipsychotics. Tactile sensitivity and tissue atrophy may also contribute. Although low testosterone was previously considered a risk factor, more recent studies found no association between ejaculation time and serum testosterone. Idiosyncratic masturbation and insufficient desire for available stimuli have also been proposed as risks. Table 6.1 groups causes of DE and anejaculation.
