document_sections.content: The table groups proposed causes under ageing, congenital, anatomic, neurogenic, infective or inflammatory, endocrine, medication-related and psychological categories.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.3 Investigation and treatment
document_sections.content: DE assessment should include a complete medical and sexual history and detailed examination. History should cover the ejaculation response, sensation, frequency, sexual activities and techniques, cultural setting, onset and course, desire, arousal, ejaculation, orgasm and refractory period, the partner's view and possible sexual dysfunction, and overall satisfaction with the relationship. Clinicians should identify contributing medical conditions by considering hormones, anatomy and general health. Evidence summaries assign LE 3 to the broad range of congenital, anatomic, neurogenic, infective, hormonal, drug-related and psychological causes and LE 3 to the conclusion that evidence does not support a definitive DE treatment.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.3.1 Psychological aspects and intervention
document_sections.content: Research on psychological aspects of DE and on psychological-treatment efficacy is scarce. Studies describe a strong wish to control sexual experiences and difficulty letting go during sexual pleasure, suggesting a psychological influence on orgasm. Possible interventions include more genital-specific stimulation, sexual education, role-play alone or with a partner, changing masturbation practices, reducing ejaculation-related or performance anxiety, and addressing a mismatch between fantasies and real-life arousal, including pornography-related stimulation. Solo or partnered masturbation may provide practice that eventually improves arousal and orgasm for both partners. Fantasy during masturbation may be harmful when disconnected from suitable arousal and context, but may help when it blocks critical thoughts that hinder orgasm and ejaculation. Anxiety-reduction skills may counter performance anxiety that interrupts normal erectile and orgasmic progression. Referral to a sexual therapist, psychologist or psychiatrist is appropriate and often warranted.

document_sections.heading: 6.3.3.2 Pharmacotherapy
document_sections.content: Cabergoline, bupropion, alpha-1-adrenergic agonists (pseudoephedrine, midodrine, imipramine and ephedrine), buspirone, oxytocin, testosterone, bethanechol, yohimbine, amantadine, cyproheptadine and apomorphine have been used for DE with variable success. No medicine is approved by the FDA or EMA for DE; much of the cited research consists of case-cohort studies without randomisation, blinding or placebo control. Drugs have been used both as primary treatment and to counter medication-induced DE. A provider survey reported 40% overall treatment success, commonly with cabergoline, bupropion or oxytocin, but represented anecdotal practitioner outcomes. No drug has proven efficacy or superiority because placebo-controlled, randomised, blinded comparative trials are lacking. Penile vibratory stimulation (PVS) is also used as an adjunct. In a study of 158 men with spinal cord injury, midodrine plus PVS produced ejaculation in almost 65%.

document_sections.heading: 6.4 Anejaculation
document_sections.content: This section defines anejaculation and describes its causes and fertility-oriented management.

document_sections.heading: 6.4.1 Definition and classification
document_sections.content: Anejaculation means complete absence of both antegrade and retrograde ejaculation because semen is not emitted from the seminal vesicles, prostate and ejaculatory ducts into the urethra. True anejaculation usually preserves orgasmic sensation and is always associated with central or peripheral nervous-system dysfunction or drugs.

document_sections.heading: 6.4.2 Pathophysiology and risk factors
document_sections.content: Anejaculation generally shares causes with DE and retrograde ejaculation; causes overlapping with DE are grouped in Table 6.1.

document_sections.heading: 6.4.3 Investigation and treatment
document_sections.content: Drug treatment for anejaculation due to lymphadenectomy or neuropathy, and psychosexual therapy for anorgasmia, are ineffective. In these circumstances and with spinal cord injury, PVS is first-line. Penile vibration triggers an ejaculation reflex requiring an intact lumbosacral spinal cord segment. If semen quality is poor or ejaculation is retrograde, couples wishing to conceive may enter an in vitro fertilisation programme. Electro-ejaculation can be selected after unsuccessful PVS; other sperm-retrieval techniques may be used if electro-ejaculation fails or is infeasible. Unilateral lymphadenectomy may prevent anejaculation after retroperitoneal surgery for testicular cancer, while autonomic nerve preservation may prevent it after total mesorectal excision.

document_sections.heading: 6.5 Painful Ejaculation
document_sections.content: This section addresses the presentation, possible causes and management of pain associated with ejaculation.

document_sections.heading: 6.5.1 Definition and classification
document_sections.content: Painful ejaculation ranges from mild discomfort to severe pain during or after ejaculation and may affect the penis, scrotum or perineum.

document_sections.heading: 6.5.2 Pathophysiology and risk factors
document_sections.content: Painful ejaculation can be idiopathic or arise with a medical condition. Reports suggest possible associations with seminal-vesicle calculi, sexual neurasthenia, STIs, prostate inflammation, PCa, BPH, prostate surgery, pelvic radiation, herniorrhaphy and antidepressants. Case reports also implicate mercury toxicity and Ciguatera toxin fish poisoning. Psychological causes may be relevant, especially when ejaculation during masturbation is painless.

document_sections.heading: 6.5.3 Investigation and treatment
document_sections.content: Management should target an identified cause. Psychotherapy or relationship counselling, withdrawal of a suspected drug, toxin or radiation exposure, or suitable antibiotics, α-blockers or anti-inflammatory agents may improve symptoms. Without an identifiable cause, options that may be implemented include behavioural therapy, muscle relaxants, antidepressants, anticonvulsants, opioids and pelvic-floor exercises.

document_sections.heading: 6.5.3.1 Surgical intervention
document_sections.content: If medical treatment fails, proposed operations include TURP, transurethral resection of the ejaculatory duct (TURED) and pudendal-nerve neurolysis. Strong evidence that surgery improves painful ejaculation is lacking, so these procedures must be used cautiously.

document_sections.heading: 6.6 Retrograde ejaculation
document_sections.content: This section describes backward movement of semen into the bladder, possible causes, drug treatment and fertility management.

document_sections.heading: 6.6.1 Definition and classification
document_sections.content: Retrograde ejaculation involves complete or sometimes partial absence of forward ejaculation because semen passes through the bladder neck into the bladder. Orgasmic sensation may be normal or diminished. Causes are described as neurogenic, pharmacological, urethral or related to bladder-neck incompetence.

document_sections.heading: 6.6.2 Pathophysiology and risk factors
document_sections.content: Normal ejaculation coordinates the epididymis, vas deferens, prostate, seminal vesicles, bladder neck and bulbourethral glands. Sperm travel rapidly through the vas deferens and ejaculatory ducts into the urethra; bladder-neck closure and rhythmic periurethral contraction support forward passage under a central reflex. The lumbar sympathetic ganglia and hypogastric nerve initiate bladder-neck closure and seminal emission. Parasympathetic signalling from S2-4 through the pelvic nerve initiates prostatic and seminal-vesicle secretion and contraction of the bulbo-cavernosal, ischio-cavernosal and pelvic-floor muscles. Disruption of this reflex or impaired internal vesical sphincter contraction may direct semen into the bladder. Table 6.2 groups reported causes.

document_sections.heading: 6.6.3 Disease management
document_sections.content: Management approaches include medicines intended to restore forward ejaculation and sperm-acquisition methods for patients concerned about infertility.

document_sections.heading: 6.6.3.1 Pharmacological
document_sections.content: Sympathomimetics promote noradrenaline release and stimulate α- and β-adrenergic receptors, closing the internal urethral sphincter and potentially restoring antegrade ejaculation. Listed agents are synephrine, pseudoephedrine hydrochloride, ephedrine, phenylpropanolamine and midodrine. Their effect diminishes over time, and efficacy studies often have small samples or consist of case reports. In an RCT after retroperitoneal lymphadenectomy, dextroamphetamine, ephedrine, phenylpropanolamine or pseudoephedrine, with or without histamine, restored antegrade ejaculation; four days of pretreatment was most effective. A systematic review estimated sympathomimetic efficacy at 28%. Adverse effects include dry mucous membranes and hypertension. Antimuscarinics such as brompheniramine maleate and imipramine have been used alone or with sympathomimetics. Calculated efficacy was 22% for antimuscarinics alone and 39% for combination therapy. Combination treatment appears more effective, but small samples preclude statistical analysis.

document_sections.heading: 6.6.3.2 Management of infertility
document_sections.content: Infertility is the principal concern for patients with retrograde ejaculation. Besides testicular sperm aspiration/extraction (TESA/TESE), described sperm-acquisition methods are centrifugation and resuspension of post-ejaculatory urine, the Hotchkiss or modified Hotchkiss technique, and ejaculation with a full bladder. For urine centrifugation, increased fluid intake or sodium bicarbonate may dilute or alkalise urine. Urine collected after orgasm by catheter or spontaneous voiding is centrifuged, and the sperm are resuspended in a medium that may contain bovine serum albumin, human serum albumin, Earle’s/Hank’s balanced salt solution or the patient's urine; the preparation can be used in assisted reproduction. A systematic review reported a 15% pregnancy rate per cycle (0-100%) with this approach. For the Hotchkiss method, a catheter empties the bladder before ejaculation; the bladder is washed and receives a small amount of Lactated Ringers, after which semen is recovered by catheterisation or voiding. Modified approaches vary the instilled medium. Reported pregnancy rates were 24% per cycle (0-100%). The full-bladder approach has the patient ejaculate with a full bladder and suspends semen in Baker’s Buffer; pregnancy results were described by two studies including only five patients, without a rate stated here.

document_sections.heading: 6.7 Anorgasmia
document_sections.content: This section discusses absent perceived orgasm, contributing factors, assessment, treatment and fertility options.

document_sections.heading: 6.7.1 Definition and classification
document_sections.content: Anorgasmia is perceived absence of orgasm and may cause anejaculation. Whether or not ejaculation occurs, it can be lifelong (primary) or acquired (secondary).

document_sections.heading: 6.7.2 Pathophysiology and risk factors
document_sections.content: Primary anorgasmia begins with the first sexual intercourse and persists throughout life; secondary anorgasmia follows a period of normal function. Reported risk factors include substance misuse, obesity, anxiety, fear and other nonspecific psychological factors. Few studies examine anorgasmia independently; it is commonly regarded as a symptom associated with ejaculatory disorders, particularly DE, and is therefore thought to share their risks. Psychological factors are considered responsible for 90% of anorgasmia problems. Table 6.3 lists causes of delayed orgasm and anorgasmia.

document_sections.content: The table groups proposed causes into endocrine conditions, medications, psychosexual causes, hyperstimulation and loss of penile sensation.

document_sections.heading: 6.7.3 Disease management
document_sections.content: Psychological and behavioural strategies resemble those for DE. Detailed physical and psychosexual assessment of the patient and partner should address onset, medicines, medical conditions, penile sensitivity and psychological concerns. Testosterone, prolactin and TSH tests may help exclude organic causes. Loss of penile sensitivity calls for further investigation.

document_sections.heading: 6.7.3.1 Psychological/behavioural strategies
document_sections.content: Lifestyle changes that may be recommended include altering masturbation style, improving intimacy and reducing alcohol intake. Offered psychotherapy methods include changing arousal techniques, reducing sexual anxiety, role-playing an exaggerated orgasm and increasing genital stimulation, alone or in combination. Available literature does not allow success rates to be determined readily.

document_sections.heading: 6.7.3.2 Pharmacotherapy
document_sections.content: Reports describe reversal of anorgasmia with cyproheptadine, yohimbine, buspirone, amantadine or oxytocin. These reports generally come from case-cohort studies, and the medicines have limited efficacy and significant adverse-effect profiles. Current evidence is therefore insufficient to recommend drug treatment for anorgasmia.

document_sections.heading: 6.7.3.3 Management of infertility
document_sections.content: If the preceding treatments fail, penile vibratory stimulation, electro-ejaculation or TESE may be used to retrieve sperm.

document_sections.heading: 6.8 Haemospermia
document_sections.content: This section addresses blood in ejaculate, possible underlying pathology, investigation, risk-based management and recommendations.

document_sections.heading: 6.8.1 Definition and classification
document_sections.content: Haemospermia means blood appearing in the ejaculate. Although often viewed as a minor symptom, it causes anxiety for many men and may signal underlying disease.

document_sections.heading: 6.8.2 Pathophysiology and risk factors
document_sections.content: Recognised causes include idiopathic, congenital, inflammatory, obstructive, malignant, vascular, traumatic or iatrogenic, and systemic conditions; Table 6.4 details associated pathology. Estimated malignancy risk among patients presenting with haemospermia is approximately 3.5% (0-13.1%). In a study of 342 patients, inflammation or infection was the most relevant cause (49.4%), whereas genitourinary cancers involving the prostate or testis accounted for 3.2%.

document_sections.heading: 6.8.3 Investigations
document_sections.content: History and assessment should seek the cause; despite an extensive differential diagnosis, most cases reflect infection or inflammation. Initial history should address the symptom and systemic health and establish whether blood truly originates in semen. Apparent haemospermia can instead reflect haematuria or a partner's blood entering the urethra during intercourse. Sexual history should assess STI risk; travel to areas affected by schistosomiasis or tuberculosis and possible hypertension, liver disease, coagulopathy, weight loss, appetite loss or bone pain should also be considered. Examination should include blood pressure because case reports suggest an association with uncontrolled hypertension. Authors broadly agree on initial investigations but have not reached consensus. Urinalysis, urine microscopy, culture and sensitivity testing are advised. If tuberculosis or schistosomiasis is suspected, semen or prostatic secretions should be analysed. A full STI screen using first-void urine, serum and genitourinary samples should test for Chlamydia, Ureaplasma and Herpes Simplex virus; this may identify infection in cases otherwise called idiopathic. Appropriately counselled men aged > 40 years should have serum PSA measured. Full blood count, liver function and clotting tests can help identify systemic disease. Decisions about further tests depend on clinical judgement, age and risk factors. Digital rectal examination is advised, with re-examination of the meatus afterwards for bloody discharge. A palpable prostatic nodule matters because an association of haemospermia with PCa has been proposed but not fully established. MRI is increasingly used to investigate haemospermia and can show structural changes in the prostate, seminal vesicles, vas-deferens ampulla and ejaculatory ducts, particularly the origin of midline or paramedian prostatic cysts and information needed for surgical planning. An endorectal coil can improve accuracy in locating and explaining bleeding. Cystoscopy is included in many proposed protocols for higher-risk patients with persistent haemospermia unresponsive to conservative treatment; direct inspection can reveal polyps, urethritis, prostatic cysts, foreign bodies, calcifications or vascular abnormalities. Small-diameter ureteroscopes permit examination of ejaculatory ducts and seminal vesicles. In a prospective study of 106 patients with prolonged haemospermia, transrectal US plus seminal vesiculoscopy established a diagnosis in 87.7%; diagnostic yields were 45.3% for TRUS and 74.5% for seminal vesiculoscopy (P < 0.001). Melanospermia due to genitourinary malignant melanoma is rare and has been reported in two case reports; semen chromatography can detect melanin when distinction is needed.

document_sections.heading: 6.8.4 Disease management
document_sections.content: Conservative care is generally the primary approach for patients aged < 40 years with a single episode. The principal aims are excluding malignancy, including prostate and bladder cancer, and treating an underlying cause; when no pathology is identified, reassurance is appropriate. Recurrent haemospermia in middle-aged patients warrants more active intervention. Patients with urogenital infection or an STI should receive appropriate antibiotics. Urethral or prostatic varices and angiodyplastic vessels may be fulgurated; seminal-vesicle or prostatic-urethral cysts may be aspirated transrectally; ejaculatory-duct obstruction may be managed by transurethral incision at its opening; and systemic conditions should receive appropriate treatment. Proposed management is based on age and extent of haemospermia, aiming to exclude uncommon serious causes such as cancer without excessive investigation while reducing anxiety. Although many causes have been described, numerous ones are uncommon after investigation. Higher-risk features include age > 40 years, recurrent or persistent bleeding, PCa risk such as a positive family history, and concurrent haematuria. A risk-based management algorithm is proposed.

document_sections.heading: Figure 6.3: Management of haemospermia [837, 840, 855, 856]
document_sections.content: The algorithm begins with history, detailed examination, blood pressure, urinalysis, urine culture, complete blood count, serum coagulation assessment, serum chemistry, semen analysis, STI screening and a condom test. Its low-risk group comprises men < 40 years old with an isolated episode and no other disease symptoms or signs; conservative treatment, watchful waiting and reassurance follow. Its high-risk group comprises men ≥ 40 years old or a man of any age with persistent haemospermia or accompanying disease symptoms or signs. For this group, identifiable causes found during routine evaluation are treated; TRUS and pelvic MRI are considered, together with PSA and DRE for prostate-cancer screening in men ≥ 40 years old and US to rule out a testicular tumour in men < 40 years old. Recurrence leads to cystourethroscopy with or without biopsy.

document_sections.heading: 6.8.5 Summary of evidence and recommendations for the investigation and management of haemospermia
document_sections.content: At LE 3, the evidence summary states that haemospermia, despite its traditional association with benign conditions, can warrant thorough diagnostic evaluation and targeted treatment when needed. At LE 3, it identifies exclusion of malignancy and treatment of other underlying causes as the main management aims. Recommendations are to obtain complete medical and sexual histories and perform a detailed physical examination (Strong), and to use risk stratification for systematic management (Weak).
